topStories.headline: Safeway Fight Moves to Fine Print: Opponents Argue the Yacht Harbor Isn't 'Urban Use'
topStories.dek: With the big legal arguments largely foreclosed by state housing law, neighbors fighting the 848-unit Marina Safeway towers are now pressing narrow technical claims in federal court.
topStories.body:
The months-long battle over Align Real Estate's proposed twin-tower redevelopment of the Marina Safeway has entered a new and more arcane phase. With California's housing-streamlining laws having stripped away most traditional avenues for blocking large residential projects, opponents of the 22-story and 18-story development at 15 Marina Blvd. are now concentrating on statutory fine print — arguing, for instance, that the Marina Yacht Harbor and Fort Mason do not qualify as the 'urban uses' that must border 75 percent of a project's perimeter for it to qualify for expedited approval under Assembly Bill 2011.

The YesAND Foundation, Neighborhoods United San Francisco, and four Marina District residents filed their federal complaint in September in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, naming the city of San Francisco, PG&E, developer Align Real Estate Partners, and Safeway parent company Albertsons as defendants. The suit contends that city officials improperly fast-tracked the 848-unit project while allowing the developer to bypass a full assessment of historical contamination from when the site housed a manufactured gas plant.

The SF Standard reported on October 20 that the Marina case has become a bellwether for how housing opponents across California are adapting after losing the broad arguments. Rather than claiming a project is too tall or out of character — objections that state law now largely overrides — challengers are zeroing in on eligibility technicalities and environmental procedural gaps. Developer Align has said the project fully complies with the law, and the San Francisco Planning Department has already ruled the project eligible under AB 2011, with a 90-day window remaining to issue final approval.

Supervisor Stephen Sherrill, who represents the Marina, Pacific Heights, Cow Hollow, and Presidio Heights, faces re-election on November 3 and has long criticized the project's scale. He is running as the strong favorite after defeating Lori Brooke — co-founder of Neighborhoods United SF, one of the groups behind the lawsuit — 70 to 30 percent in the June special election.

topStories.headline: Presidio Heights Resident's Viral Video Asks: Are Neighbors Faking Construction to Hoard Street Parking?
topStories.dek: A local history buff counted 14 no-parking signs on one side of his block and found the city's temporary street space permit is surprisingly easy — and cheap — to obtain.
topStories.body:
Greg Long, a 56-year-old product designer and amateur neighborhood historian who documents Presidio Heights mansions on Instagram, posted a video this week that quickly went viral: standing on his block along Jackson Street, he counted roughly a dozen red-and-white construction tow-away signs and wondered aloud how many were backed by real renovation work.

Long looked into the city's temporary street space permit system and found that San Francisco Public Works issues the permits — which block off curbside parking during posted hours — for $209 per 20 linear feet per month, with an $851 upfront application fee. Crucially, the permits can be obtained for landscaping without any construction permit or submitted documents, and Public Works told him it does not typically require verification paperwork before issuing them. In a neighborhood where private parking can cost far more each month, that math is striking to residents already struggling for curb space.

The San Francisco Chronicle and KTVU both covered the story on October 20. Public Works pushed back, saying permit abuse is not widespread and that it investigates complaints. The agency said it can levy fines of up to $1,000 per day for misuse and urged anyone who suspects an expired or fraudulent permit to report it through the city's 311 service. Long acknowledged that most permits on his block are probably legitimate, but his video had clearly touched a nerve — commenters reported similar frustrations on blocks throughout Pacific Heights and the Marina.

topStories.headline: Hamlin School Files Plans for a Four-Story Addition Next to Its 125-Year-Old Pacific Heights Mansion
topStories.dek: The all-girls K–8 school on Broadway wants to replace a play area with a new academic building featuring art studios, a maker's space, and multipurpose classrooms.
topStories.body:
The Hamlin School filed plans with the San Francisco Planning Department this month for a new four-story academic building at 2120 Broadway, directly beside Stanwood Hall — the 1901 mansion that has anchored the school's Pacific Heights campus since 1923. Hoodline and SF YIMBY reported on the filing on October 17.

The proposed structure, designed by Mark Cavagnero Associates — the firm that led the school's 2022 full-campus renovation — would rise 39 feet on a parcel Hamlin purchased in 2006 that currently serves as a play area. The roughly 8,140-square-foot building would include art rooms, a maker's studio, multipurpose rooms, and classrooms, expanding the campus's total built footprint to about 78,840 square feet. Plans also call for improvements to the lowest level of historic Stanwood Hall, including upgraded classrooms and restrooms and a new entry door.

The proposal would reduce on-site car parking by two spaces, accommodating 25 bicycles and 12 cars — a trade-off reflecting both the tight footprint of one of Pacific Heights' steepest blocks and a stated preference for active transportation. Hamlin, which describes itself as the oldest nonsectarian school for girls in the western United States, serves students in kindergarten through eighth grade. The new building would require city planning approval before any construction could begin.

moreNews.headline: Marina Harbor Dredging in Final Days; Weekly Channel Soundings Suspended This Week
moreNews.body: West-entrance dredging at the San Francisco Marina Yacht Harbor, which began October 17, is running through its expected ten-day window. The harbor's October 22 weekly update — the most recent posted to the SF Rec & Park page — notes that active equipment in the middle of the channel prevented the usual Thursday sounding report. Weekly soundings are expected to resume next week. Boaters should continue to navigate with caution; harbor staff will post an announcement when dredging concludes.
moreNews.sourceName: SF Recreation & Parks — Marina Yacht Harbor
